question: to the Vice-President of the Commission / High Representative of the Union for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Erik Kaliňák (NI) Subject:

In April 2026, the European Union adopted the 20th package of sanctions against the Russian Federation, and the Member States are already discussing a further sanctions package. At the same time, EU expenditure on support for Ukraine continues to rise. Against this background, the EU is facing slowing growth, increasing budgetary pressure and deteriorating competitiveness. I would therefore like to ask: 1.
What specific measurable indicators does the European External Action Service use when assessing the effectiveness of sanctions?

What results has the 20th sanctions package produced in terms of the Russian Federation’s revenue from energy exports? I am not interested in claims that ‘sanctions are working’; I want to know how and to what benefit, in figures.
Has the EEAS carried out, or commissioned, an analysis of the economic impact of the sanctions on the individual Member States, including the Slovak Republic?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (13.7.2026) In response to Russia’s unprovoked and unjustified military aggression against Ukraine, the EU has imposed unprecedented restrictive measures against Russia. Those measures are designed to reduce the Kremlin’s ability to finance the war, impose clear economic and political costs on Russia’s political elite, while increasing the long-term economic costs of its aggression. Russia’s economy is showing increasing signs of strain. In the first quarter of 2026, real gross domestic product (GDP) contracted by 0.2%, while the key interest rate remains very high (currently at 14.25%), keeping the cost of capital elevated and constraining investment and growth. Outstanding corporate loan debt in Russia has nearly doubled since the start of the war, heightening credit risks in the banking sector and adding to broader macroeconomic fragility. At the same time, despite rising defence expenditure and higher oil prices, Russia’s fiscal position has deteriorated sharply. By end May 2026, the budget deficit reached 6 trillion RUB, equivalent to 2.6% of GDP. This is more than the deficit recorded for the whole 2025 and already 50% above the entire deficit planned for 2026. Furthermore, Russian fossil fuel revenues are almost one third lower than pre-invasion levels. EU sanctions are designed to maximise pressure on Russia while minimising unintended consequences for the EU and the rest of the world. Restrictive measures are regularly reviewed, amended and renewed by the Council by unanimity, in the light of political developments on the ground.
